title: Detection and defense mirror
status: AUTHORED. The other half. Every offensive entry elsewhere in this repo is supposed to have a row here.

atom_notes.A01: interpreter confusion is the most detectable class, because the payload shape is unusual
atom_notes.A02: trust boundary crossing is detectable at the decision point, if the decision is logged with both identities
atom_notes.A16: model and agent manipulation is the least mature detection area and the one with the most vendor claims

required_cells.why: report the detection that would catch the technique, not just the technique
verify the control after the fix, which is a detection question

entries.name: Sigma
entries.role: The vendor neutral detection rule format. If your finding has no Sigma rule, detection coverage is a guess

entries.name: Suricata
entries.role: Network IDS with rules per attack class, the wire level mirror

entries.name: YARA
entries.role: Pattern matching for artefacts, used here for payload and malware signatures

entries.name: OWASP Core Rule Set
entries.role: The CRS rule family most WAFs run, so 'which CRS rule catches this' is the real question
entries.note: The highest value defensive artefact in this domain. A bypass that still trips a CRS rule is not a bypass.

entries.name: Wazuh
entries.role: Host and log based detection with a free SIEM, the SMB default

entries.name: Zeek
entries.role: Network analysis framework, the source of the session logs that rules run on

entries.name: Falco
entries.role: Runtime detection for containers and cloud native workloads

entries.name: Elastic detection rules
entries.role: A large maintained rule set, useful as a coverage cross check

entries.name: ATT&CK STIX data
entries.role: The technique taxonomy to map detection coverage against

entries.name: This repo: counters/COUNTERS.md
entries.role: 74 control mechanisms across 150 patterns, grouped into 13 classes, each with a precondition and cost
entries.note: Local document in web-attack-atlas. It is the defensive view of the pattern corpus.

tree.q: Are you writing the finding, or the detection?
tree.why: Both are in scope and they use the same corpus from opposite directions. A finding says what is broken. A detection says how you would know. This repo insists on both because a finding with no detection is unactionable at scale.

branches.action: attach the CRS rule family that would catch it, or state that none would, which is itself a finding about the defence
branches.oracle: a rule identifier that fires on the proving request

branches.action: write the Sigma rule against the behaviour, not the payload string, then test it against the proving request and a benign control
branches.oracle: rule fires on the attack and not on the control

branches.action: map existing rules to ATT&CK techniques, then look for techniques with no rule and no log source
Falco for containers, Zeek for wire, Wazuh for host and log
branches.oracle: alert on the technique with the entity recorded

mirror.detect: the rule named in its detected_by field
mirror.control: the counter named in its counter field

mirror.detect: a technique with no rule and no log source
rule matches a string that an encoding change defeats
mirror.control: write against behaviour and parser state

gaps.gap: No automatic link between the pattern corpus and a rule set
gaps.build_candidate: emit a Sigma stub per pattern from its detected_by field, then hand tune

gaps.gap: No coverage test that proves a rule fires on the attack and not on the control
gaps.build_candidate: replay harness with a benign control per rule
